ARTICLE: Amateur radio
WIKIPEDIA REVISION TEXT

{{Short description|Non-commercial use of the radio spectrum}}
{{Redirect|Ham radio|other uses|Ham radio (disambiguation)}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=November 2019}}
[[File:Amateurfunkstation.jpg|thumb|Amateur radio station with transceivers, amplifiers, and a computer for digital modes. On the wall are awards, certificates, and [[QSL card]]s from foreign stations]]

'''Amateur radio''', also known as '''ham radio''', is the use of specific bands and frequencies within the [[radio spectrum]] for non-commercial communication, technical experimentation, self-training, recreation, [[radiosport]], [[contesting]], and [[Amateur radio emergency communications|emergency communications]].<ref name=Silver-2021>{{Cite book |last=Silver |first=H. Ward |title=Ham Radio For Dummies |date=2021 |publisher=Wiley |isbn=978-1-119-69576-9 |edition=4th |location=Hoboken, NJ |oclc=1245417767 }}</ref> A surge of popular interest in radio experimentation in the early 20th century necessitated that parts of the radio spectrum be allocated to non-professionals. In 1927 a ''radio amateur'' was defined as "a duly authorized person interested in radioelectric practice with a purely personal aim and without [[wikt:pecuniary|pecuniary]] interest", meaning without monetary or similar reward. The definition distinguished amateur activity from [[commercial broadcasting]], public safety services, and professional [[two-way radio]] uses such as maritime, aviation, and taxi communication.<ref>{{cite web |date=1928 |title=General Regulations Annexed to the International Radiotelegraph Convention |website=International Radiotelegraph Convention of Washington, 1927 |publisher=His Majesty's Stationery Office |pages=29–172 |location=London, UK |url=https://www.itu.int/dms_pub/itu-s/oth/02/02/S02020000204501PDFE.pdf |access-date=4 June 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170728130153/https://www.itu.int/dms_pub/itu-s/oth/02/02/S02020000204501PDFE.pdf |archive-date=28 July 2017 }}</ref>

[[File:Krótkofalowiec polski, SP1QE.jpg|thumb|Polish amateur radio station SP1QE with a 1930s [[vacuum tube]] transmitter and receiver]]

The amateur radio service (''amateur service'' and ''[[amateur-satellite service]]'') is established by the [[International Telecommunication Union]] (ITU) through its [[Radio Regulations]]. National governments set technical and operational rules for transmissions and issue individual station licences with unique [[call sign]]s. Call signs must be used in transmissions, at least every ten minutes and at the end of the conversation. [[Amateur radio operator]]s must hold an [[#Licensing|amateur radio licence]], granted after an examination that tests knowledge of radio theory, [[electronics]], and national regulations.

Operators are authorised to transmit on frequency ranges allocated internationally as the ''[[amateur radio band|amateur radio bands]]''. Within these bands they may use any [[frequency]], though some are restricted to particular modes of voice, text, image, or [[data communication]]s. Additionally, some frequencies are restricted to lower maximum power outputs. This allows communication locally, nationally, worldwide, and even with stations in space. In many countries, operators may also exchange radio communications between [[computer]]s or [[transceiver]]s connected through [[virtual private network]]s on the [[Internet]].

Amateur radio is represented by the [[International Amateur Radio Union]] (IARU), which has three regions and includes national amateur radio societies in most countries. In 2011 the [[American Radio Relay League]] (the U.S. national society) estimated that about 2&nbsp;million people worldwide were active in amateur radio.<ref>{{cite magazine |last=Sumner |first=David |date=August 2011 |title=How Many Hams? |magazine=QST |publisher=[[American Radio Relay League]] |page=9 }}</ref> About 830,000 [[amateur radio station]]s are in [[International Amateur Radio Union#IARU Region 2|Region&nbsp;2]] (the Americas), about 750,000 in [[International Amateur Radio Union#IARU Region 3|Region&nbsp;3]] (South and East Asia and the Pacific), and about 400,000 in [[International Amateur Radio Union#IARU Region 1|Region&nbsp;1]] (Europe, the Middle East, the [[Commonwealth of Independent States|CIS]] and Africa). Radio amateurs have been credited with a number of advances, notably the discovery of [[skywave]] propagation.

==History==
{{main|History of amateur radio}}
[[File:mw0rkbshack.jpg|thumb|right|An amateur radio station in [[Wales]]. Multiple transceivers are employed for different bands and modes. Computers are used for control, data modes, SDR, RTTY and logging.]]
<!--Please do not add extensive info to this section; instead, go to the "History of Amateur Radio" page-->
The origins of amateur radio can be traced to the late 19th century, but amateur radio as practised today began in the early 20th century. The ''First Annual Official Wireless Blue Book of the Wireless Association of America'', produced in 1909, contains a list of amateur radio stations.<ref name="bluebook1909">{{Cite book |last=Gernsback |first=H |url=https://w3abt.seas.upenn.edu/wp-content/uploads/2019/01/First-Annual-Official-Wireless-Blue-Book-1909.pdf |title=First Annual Official Wireless Blue Book of the Wireless Association of America |date=May 1909 |publisher=Modern Electrics Publication |location=[[New York City|New York]] |access-date=19 June 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100706002250/http://www.seas.upenn.edu/~uparc/documents/First%20Annual%20Official%20Wireless%20Blue%20Book%20-%201909.pdf |archive-date=6 July 2010 |url-status=live}}</ref> This radio [[callbook]] lists [[wireless telegraph]] stations in Canada and the United States, including 89 amateur radio stations. As with radio in general, amateur radio was associated with various amateur experimenters and hobbyists. Amateur radio enthusiasts have significantly contributed to [[science]], [[engineering]], industry, and [[social services]]. Research by amateur operators has founded new industries, like experimentation with quartz [[crystal oscillator|piezoelectric resonators]] from 1924 until about 1934,<ref>{{cite conference |last=Brown |first=Patrick R.J. |date=5–7 June 1996 |title=The influence of amateur radio on the development of the commercial market for quartz piezoelectric resonators in the United States |book-title=Proceedings of 1996 IEEE International Frequency Control Symposium |conference=1996 IEEE International Frequency Control Symposium |location=Honolulu, HI |publisher=[[Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers]] (IEEE) |pages=58–65 |doi=10.1109/FREQ.1996.559819 |isbn=0-7803-3309-8 |publication-date=1996 |url=http://www.bliley.net/XTAL/Industry-Hams.html |url-status=live |access-date=22 December 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130113003917/http://www.bliley.net/XTAL/Industry-Hams.html |archive-date=13 January 2013 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> built economies,<ref>{{cite web |title=Inventor of IC 'chip', Nobel Prize winner Jack S. Kilby credits amateur radio for his start in electronics |date=20 June 2005 |url=http://nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/physics/laureates/2000/kilby-autobio.html |url-status=live |via=Nobelprize.org |access-date=22 November 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121105132023/http://www.nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/physics/laureates/2000/kilby-autobio.html |archive-date=5 November 2012 }}</ref> empowered nations,<ref>{{cite report |first=Bazlur |last=Rahman |date=2004-07-19 |title=Role of amateur radio in development communication of Bangladesh |department=Information & Communication Technology for Development (ICT4D) |series=Bangladesh NGOs Network for Radio & Communication (BNNRC) |location=Blacksburg, VA |publisher=[[Virginia Tech]] |url=http://www.cimap.vt.edu/files/internet/Impression/ICT.pdf |via=cimap.vt.edu |access-date=11 May 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150518092904/http://www.cimap.vt.edu/files/internet/Impression/ICT.pdf |archive-date=18 May 2015 }}</ref> and saved lives in times of emergency.<ref>{{cite news |last=Taylor |first=Jim |date=2004-12-29 |title=Amateur radio "saved lives" in south Asia |periodical=Canadian Amateur Radio Bulletin |publisher=[[Radio Amateurs of Canada]] |url=http://www.hfradio.net/bulletin/jan0205i.html |via=Hfradio.net |access-date=22 November 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120306182700/http://www.hfradio.net/bulletin/jan0205i.html |archive-date=6 March 2012 }}</ref><ref name=ARRL-whatis>{{cite web |title=What is ham radio? |website=[[American Radio Relay League]] |url=http://www.arrl.org/what-is-ham-radio |url-status=live |access-date=1 June 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100504001349/http://www.arrl.org/what-is-ham-radio-1 |archive-date=4 May 2010 }}</ref> Ham radio can also be used in the classroom to teach English, map skills, geography, math, science, and computer skills.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Weaver |first=Bruce D. |date=January 2003 |title=On the Air Learning |journal=Teaching Pre K-8 |volume=33 |issue=4 |pages=50–51 |issn=0891-4508 }}</ref>

===Ham radio===
{{main|Etymology of ham radio|l1=Etymology of ''ham radio''}}
The term ''ham'' was originally a [[pejorative]], used in professional [[telegraph|wired telegraphy]] during the 19th&nbsp;century to mock operators with poor [[Morse code]]-sending skills ("[[wikt:ham-fisted|ham-fisted]]").<ref>{{cite magazine |title=Ham fisted |date=August 1972 |magazine=[[QST]] magazine |page=83 |publisher=[[ARRL]] }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Brady |first=Jasper Ewing |year=1899 |title=Tales of the Telegraph |publisher=Doubleday & McClure |oclc=3421513 |url=https://archive.org/details/talesoftelegraph00bradiala }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Ham radio history |website=[[American Radio Relay League]] |url=http://www.arrl.org/ham-radio-history |url-status=live |access-date=17 April 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150510223641/http://www.arrl.org/ham-radio-history |archive-date=10 May 2015 }}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine |last=Hall |first=L.C. |date=January 1902 |title=Telegraph talk and talkers: The slang of the wire |magazine=[[McClure's|McClure's Magazine]] |volume=18 |issue=3 |page=231 |url=https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=uc1.a0013869276;view=1up;seq=241 }}</ref> This term continued to be used after the invention of radio and the subsequent proliferation of amateur experimentation with wireless telegraphy; among both land-based and sea-based professional radio telegraphers, ''ham'' amateurs were considered a nuisance. The use of ''ham'' to mean amateurish or unskilled survives to this day in another discipline— i.e. ''ham actor''.

The amateur radio community subsequently reclaimed the word as a label of pride,<ref>{{cite magazine |editor-last=Warner |editor-first=Kenneth B. |date=January 1920 |title=QST subscription contest |magazine=[[QST]] magazine |publisher=[[American Radio Relay League]] |volume=3 |issue=6 |pages=32–33 |url=https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?title=File:January_1920_QST.djvu&page=29 }}</ref> and by the mid-20th&nbsp;century it had lost its pejorative meaning. Although not an acronym or initialism, it is occasionally written as "HAM" in capital letters.

== Activity and practice ==
Amateur radio combines communication, technical experimentation, and recreation. Operators take part in contests, provide emergency service, build and modify equipment, and use transmission modes ranging from traditional Morse code to modern digital protocols.

[[File:Sp5hnk oh0.jpg|thumb|right|Amateur operator with antennas in [[Åland]]]]

=== Community and social use ===
[[File:Ham radio antenna tower.jpg|thumb|right|Backyard amateur radio antenna farm]]
Operators often join conversational groups and take part in scheduled on-air meetings called [[Amateur radio net|nets]], coordinated by a net control station.<ref name="netcontrol">{{cite web |last=Haag |first=Jerry |title=Principles of Amateur Radio Net Control |url=http://www.scc-ares-races.org/mtnview/principles-of-net-control.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060507132245/http://www.scc-ares-races.org/mtnview/principles-of-net-control.html |archive-date=7 May 2006 |access-date=10 January 2007 |website=SCC-AREA-RACES.org}}</ref> Nets may provide training for emergencies, operate as informal discussions, or focus on specialised topics.<ref>{{cite conference |last=Kinsner |first=Witold |title=Enhanced crowdsourcing for disasters through ham-radio operators |conference=2014 IEEE Canada International Humanitarian Technology Conference (IHTC) |publisher=IEEE |location=Montreal |date=2014 |pages=1–6 |doi=10.1109/IHTC.2014.7147544 |s2cid=20132820 |isbn=978-1-4799-3996-1}}</ref>

With battery- or generator-powered equipment, operators frequently provide communication during natural disasters when commercial services are unavailable.<ref>{{cite book |last=Edwards |first=Lynn Ellen |title=The Utilization of Amateur Radio in Disaster Communications |series=Working paper |volume=86 |publisher=University of Colorado, Boulder. Natural Hazards Research and Applications Information Center / DIANE Publishing |date=1994 |isbn=0-7881-1097-7}}</ref>

Competitive activities include contests to contact as many stations as possible in a set period, and operating awards such as [[Summits on the Air]], [[Worked All States]], and [[Jamboree on the Air]]. Operators also contribute to [[citizen science]] by collecting propagation data and supporting [[atmospheric science]] research.<ref>{{cite web |title=Radio Blackout! Ham Radio as an Operational and Scientific Instrument |date=16 February 2015 |url=https://eos.org/research-spotlights/radio-blackout-ham-radio-operational-scientific-instrument |website=EOS |access-date=10 January 2025}}</ref>

==Radiotelephony==
The principal voice modes are [[frequency modulation]] (FM), [[single-sideband modulation|single sideband]] (SSB), and [[amplitude modulation]] (AM). FM offers high audio quality, SSB is efficient for long-distance use,<ref>{{cite web |title=Radio Amateurs |department=Other spectrum topics |series=ECC Topics |publisher=European Conference of Postal and Telecommunications Administrations |website=CEPT.org |url=https://cept.org/ecc/topics/radio-amateurs |access-date=5 April 2024}}</ref> and AM continues among users of [[vintage amateur radio]] equipment.

==Radiotelegraphy==
[[Telegraphy|Radiotelegraphy]] using [[International Morse code]], or [[continuous wave]] (CW), is one of the oldest modes in amateur radio. Although largely replaced in professional services, it remains in use on [[shortwave]] bands because it functions under weak-signal conditions and employs internationally understood codes such as the [[Q code]]. CW is also used by hobbyists who build their own equipment ([[Amateur radio homebrew|home construction]]) and by operators engaged in [[QRP operation|low-power operation]], as CW transmitters are simple to construct and weak signals can often be received by ear.

Until 2003, Morse code proficiency was required under international regulations for access to frequencies below 30&nbsp;MHz.<ref name="fcc06-178a1">{{cite web |title=FCC Report and Order 06-178A1 |url=http://hraunfoss.fcc.gov/edocs_public/attachmatch/FCC-06-178A1.pdf |publisher=Federal Communications Commission |date=19 December 2006 |page=7 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111019174829/http://hraunfoss.fcc.gov/edocs_public/attachmatch/FCC-06-178A1.pdf |archive-date=19 October 2011 |access-date=16 May 2007}}</ref> The requirement was withdrawn in the United States in 2007.<ref name=e7-729>{{cite journal |title=47 CFR Part 97 |journal=Federal Register |volume=72 |issue=15 |pages=3081–3082 |publisher=Government Printing Office |date=24 January 2007 |url=http://edocket.access.gpo.gov/2007/pdf/E7-729.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080216095957/http://edocket.access.gpo.gov/2007/pdf/E7-729.pdf |archive-date=16 February 2008 |access-date=18 December 2007}}</ref><ref name=morsedropped1>{{cite news |title=FCC to drop Morse testing for all amateur license classes |date=19 December 2006 |work=American Radio Relay League |url=http://www.arrl.org/news/stories/2006/12/15/104/?nc=1 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100131103003/http://www.arrl.org/news/stories/2006/12/15/104/?nc=1 |archive-date=31 January 2010 |access-date=3 May 2025}}</ref>{{efn-ua|The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) officially ended the Morse code proficiency test for all amateur radio license classes on
February 23, 2007. 
The transition occurred in several stages over the preceding decades: 

    1991: The FCC first introduced a "no-code" Technician Class license, though code proficiency was still required to access frequencies below 30 MHz.
    2000: The requirement for higher-level licenses (General and Amateur Extra) was standardized and reduced to a single speed of 5 words per minute (WPM).
    2003: The International Telecommunication Union (ITU) modified international regulations, leaving it to individual countries to decide if Morse code should remain a requirement.
    December 15, 2006: The FCC released the official Report and Order announcing the total elimination of the Morse code exam.
    February 23, 2007: The new rules became effective, allowing applicants to earn any class of license by passing only the written theory examinations.}}

=== Digital and computer-assisted modes ===
Personal computers have enabled new digital transmission modes. [[Radioteletype]] (RTTY), once operated by mechanical devices,<ref name=Missouri>{{cite web |title=Radio room photos |website=KH6BB USS Missouri Battleship Radio Room |url=http://www.kh6bb.org/photos1.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101216035321/http://www.kh6bb.org/photos1.html |archive-date=16 December 2010 |access-date=23 May 2010}}</ref> is now handled in software. Packet radio, developed in the 1970s, uses protocols such as [[AX.25]] and [[Internet protocol suite|TCP/IP]]. Later modes including [[PSK31]] and [[FT8]] allow efficient low-signal communication on shortwave bands.

[[Radio over IP]] (RoIP) applies Internet-based telephony techniques to radio. [[EchoLink]] and the [[Internet Radio Linking Project]] link repeaters and operators worldwide.<ref>{{cite web |last=Valdes |first=Robert |title=Use of VoIP in amateur radio |date=9 May 2001 |website=HowStuffWorks |url=http://communication.howstuffworks.com/ip-telephony10.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120114173645/http://communication.howstuffworks.com/ip-telephony10.htm |archive-date=14 January 2012 |access-date=22 November 2012}}</ref>  

Other specialised modes support weak-signal communication. [[Automatic link establishment]] (ALE) maintains networks on [[high frequency|high-frequency]] bands, while the [[WSJT (Amateur radio software)|WSJT]] suite supports [[meteor burst communications|meteor scatter]] and [[Earth–Moon–Earth communication|moonbounce]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Deacon |first1=Chris |last2=Mitchell |first2=Cathryn |last3=Watson |first3=Robert |title=Consolidated amateur radio signal reports as indicators of intense sporadic E layers |journal=Atmosphere |volume=13 |issue=6 |page=906 |date=2 June 2022 |doi=10.3390/atmos13060906 |issn=2073-4433 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2022Atmos..13..906D }}</ref>

=== Television and repeater systems ===
Fast-scan [[amateur television]] (ATV) adapts consumer video equipment to transmit images. It typically operates on the [[70-centimeter band|70&nbsp;cm]] (420–450&nbsp;MHz) but may also use the [[33-centimeter band|33&nbsp;cm]] and higher frequencies. Because of wide bandwidth requirements, ATV usually covers 30–100&nbsp;km (20–60&nbsp;mi). Linked [[repeater]] systems extend this range to several hundred kilometres.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Taggart |first=Ralph E. |title=An introduction to amateur television |journal=QST |publisher=ARRL |date=April 1993 |pages=19–23 |url=http://www.arrl.org/tis/info/pdf/49319.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070605111732/http://www.arrl.org/tis/info/pdf/49319.pdf |archive-date=5 June 2007 |access-date=10 January 2025}}</ref> Repeaters are often located on high ground or towers and may be linked by other amateur bands, landlines, or the Internet.

=== Space and atmospheric propagation ===
[[File:ISS-24 Doug Wheelock uses ham radio system 1.jpg|thumb|right|NASA astronaut [[Doug Wheelock]] using amateur radio aboard the [[International Space Station]]]]  
Operators can use [[amateur radio satellite]]s, sometimes with only a hand-held transceiver.<ref>{{cite web |last=Holmstead |first=Stephen |title=Amateur Satellite FAQ |date=30 December 1994 |url=http://www.amsat.org/amsat/intro/sats_faq.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100106121014/http://www.amsat.org/amsat/intro/sats_faq.html |archive-date=6 January 2010 |access-date=14 March 2010 |publisher=The Radio Amateur Satellite Corporation}}</ref> Natural reflectors such as the [[Moon]], the [[aurora borealis]], and [[meteor]] trails are also used.<ref name=WJST>{{cite journal |last=Taylor |first=Joe |title=''WSJT'': New software for VHF meteor-scatter communication |journal=QST |publisher=ARRL |date=December 2001 |pages=36–41 |url=http://www.arrl.org/tis/info/pdf/0112036.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090324235719/http://www.arrl.org/tis/info/pdf/0112036.pdf |archive-date=24 March 2009 |access-date=10 January 2025}}</ref> Licensed astronauts have also made contacts from the [[International Space Station]] through the [[ARISS]] programme.<ref name=ARISS>{{cite web |title=ARISS: Amateur radio on the International Space Station |website=ARRL.org |publisher=American Radio Relay League |url=http://www.arrl.org/ARISS/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070111032250/http://www.arrl.org/ARISS/ |archive-date=11 January 2007 |access-date=10 January 2007}}</ref><ref name="astrohams">{{cite web |last=Jurrens |first=Gerald |title=Astronaut (and Former Astronaut) Hams |url=http://users.tellurian.com/gjurrens/astrohams.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061230122251/http://users.tellurian.com/gjurrens/astrohams.html |archive-date=30 December 2006 |access-date=10 January 2007 |website=Tellurian.com}}</ref>

== Licensing ==  

Because radio signals can propagate across national borders, amateur radio is regulated by governments under international frameworks.<ref>{{cite book |last=Hendy |first=David |title=Radio in the Global Age |publisher=Polity Press; Blackwell Publishers |location=Cambridge; Malden, MA |date=2000 |isbn=978-0-7456-2068-8}}</ref> National requirements generally follow standards set by the [[International Telecommunication Union]] (ITU)<ref name="ituars">{{cite web |title=Amateur and Amateur-satellite service |publisher=International Telecommunication Union |url=http://life.itu.int/radioclub/ars.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100822233356/http://life.itu.int/radioclub/ars.htm |archive-date=22 August 2010 |access-date=16 August 2010}}</ref> and [[World Radiocommunication Conference|World Radiocommunication Conferences]].  

Most countries require candidates to pass an examination that tests electronics, radio propagation, operating practices, and regulations.<ref>{{cite web |title=Minimum Qualifications For Radio Amateurs |website=International Telecommunication Union |date=1 May 2000 |url=http://www.itu.int/rec/R-REC-M.1544/e |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121012203747/http://www.itu.int/rec/R-REC-M.1544/e |archive-date=12 October 2012 |access-date=22 November 2012}}</ref> Licensing grants access to a broader portion of the spectrum, additional communication modes, and higher transmitter power than unlicensed personal radio services such as [[Citizens band radio|CB]], [[Family Radio Service|FRS]], or [[PMR446]].<ref>{{cite conference |last=Kasser |first=J. E. |title=Amateur radio: Past, present and future |conference=International Conference on 100 Years of Radio |publisher=IEE |date=1995 |pages=120–127 |doi=10.1049/cp:19950801 |isbn=978-0-85296-649-5}}</ref>  

[[File:Montreal-tower-top.thumb2-crop.jpg|thumb|left|The top of a tower supporting a [[Yagi–Uda antenna]] and several wire antennas, along with a Canadian flag]]  

Examination systems often include several levels, each granting wider frequency access and higher power limits.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Segal |first=Paul M. |title=The Regulation of Amateur Radio Communication |journal=Air Law Review |volume=2 |pages=153–170 |date=1931 |url=https://heinonline.org/HOL/Page?handle=hein.journals/airlr2&id=165}}</ref><ref name=Rappaport-2022>{{cite journal |last=Rappaport |first=Theodore S. |title=Crucible of Communications: How Amateur Radio Launched the Information Age and Brought High Tech to Life. Part 1: The Birth and Breadth of the Ham Radio Hobby |journal=IEEE Communications Magazine |volume=60 |issue=10 |pages=6–10 |date=2022 |doi=10.1109/MCOM.2022.9928087 |issn=0163-6804 |bibcode=2022IComM..60j...6R}}</ref> In the United Kingdom and Australia, entry-level candidates used to have to complete a practical skills test to obtain the Foundation Licence, the first of three licensing stages.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Wait |first=Phil |title=Not your grandfather's HAM radio |journal=Journal of Telecommunications and the Digital Economy |volume=3 |issue=4 |pages=155–165 |date=2015 |doi=10.18080/jtde.v3n4.41 |doi-access=free}}</ref>  

Each licensee is normally assigned a unique [[call sign]].<ref>{{cite conference |last1=Bogdan |first1=Cristian |last2=Bowers |first2=John |title=Tuning In: Challenging Design for Communities through a Field Study of Radio Amateurs |book-title=Communities and Technologies 2007 |editor-last=Steinfield |editor-first=Charles |editor2-last=Pentland |editor2-first=Brian T. |editor3-last=Ackerman |editor3-first=Mark |editor4-last=Contractor |editor4-first=Noshir |publisher=Springer |location=London |pages=439–461 |date=2007 |doi=10.1007/978-1-84628-905-7_22 |isbn=978-1-84628-904-0 |bibcode=2007cat..book..439B}}</ref> Some countries issue additional station licences, or recognise club and organisational licences.<ref name="CQ现代通信">{{cite magazine |title=见证共和国业余无线电发展的人：专访童晓勇/BA1AA |trans-title=Interview with Tong Xiaoyong (BA1AA), a witness to the development of amateur radio in the PRC |magazine=CQ现代通信 |publisher=北京博趣出版有限责任公司 |language=zh |issue=2017–2 |page=65 |issn=1000-6559}}</ref>  

[[File:ICOM IC-P7 dscn2510a.jpg|thumb|right|A handheld [[Very high frequency|VHF]]/[[Ultra high frequency|UHF]] [[transceiver]]]]  

Licences are generally valid only in the issuing country or in states with reciprocal agreements.<ref>{{cite journal |last=de la Cruz Silveira Zavala |first=J. |title=A new CITEL fosters telecommunications in the Americas |journal=IEEE Communications Magazine |volume=33 |issue=9 |pages=128–131 |date=1995 |doi=10.1109/35.408437 |bibcode=1995IComM..33i.128D }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last=Lin |first=Chun Hung |title=Regionalism or Globalism: The Process of Telecommunication Cooperation within the OAS and NAFTA |journal=Currents: International Trade Law Journal |volume=11 |pages=30–46 |date=2002 |url=https://heinonline.org/HOL/Page?handle=hein.journals/curritlj11&id=128}}</ref> In some jurisdictions, a licence is also required to purchase or possess amateur radio equipment.<ref>{{cite web |title=Amateur radio licensing in Thailand: The equipment licence |publisher=Radio Amateur Society of Thailand |date=7 August 2010 |url=http://www.qsl.net/rast/text/licensing2010.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110226041031/http://www.qsl.net/rast/text/licensing2010.html |archive-date=26 February 2011 |access-date=13 February 2011}}</ref>  

{{Further|Amateur radio licensing in the United States}}
In the United States, the [[Federal Communications Commission]] (FCC) issues three licence classes: Technician, General, and Amateur Extra.<ref name="FCC Amateur Exam">{{cite web |title=Amateur Licensing Examinations |publisher=Federal Communications Commission |url=http://wireless.fcc.gov/services/index.htm?job=licensing_2&id=amateur |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160529221252/http://wireless.fcc.gov/services/index.htm?job=licensing_2&id=amateur |archive-date=29 May 2016 |access-date=23 May 2016}}</ref> Examinations are administered by accredited Volunteer Examiners through the FCC's Volunteer Examiner Coordinator system. Higher licence classes provide access to more frequency bands and higher transmitter power. The tests cover regulations, operating practices, electronics theory, equipment design, and safety. Morse code is no longer tested. Licences are valid for ten years, and the national question pools are published in advance and updated every four years.<ref name="FCC Amateur Exam"/>

===Licensing requirements===
Prospective amateur radio operators are examined on understanding of the key concepts of electronics, radio equipment, antennas, [[radio propagation]], [[Radio frequency|RF]] safety, and the radio regulations of the government granting the license.<ref name=Silver-2021/> These examinations are sets of questions typically posed in either a short answer or multiple-choice format. Examinations can be administered by [[bureaucrat]]s, non-paid certified examiners, or previously licensed amateur radio operators.<ref name=Silver-2021/>

The ease with which an individual can acquire an amateur radio license varies from country to country. In some countries, examinations may be offered only once or twice a year in the national capital and can be inordinately bureaucratic (for example in India) or challenging because some amateurs must undergo difficult security approval (as in [[Iran]]). Currently, only [[Yemen]] and [[North Korea]] do not issue amateur radio licenses to their citizens.<ref>Bovitz, J. S. (2017). Travels and Adventures in Ham Radio with Hon. John T. Laney III. ''American Bankruptcy Institute Journal'', ''36''(4), 54.</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Ward |first=John |date=2021-06-29 |title=Bouncing signals off the moon: Amateur Radio Club draws young and experienced 'ham' operators |url=https://cdispatch.com/news/bouncing-signals-off-the-moon-amateur-radio-club-draws-young-and-experienced-ham-operators/ |access-date=2024-07-21 |website=The Dispatch |language=en-US}}</ref> Some developing countries, especially those in Africa, Asia, and [[Latin America]], require the payment of annual license fees that can be prohibitively expensive for most of their citizens. A few small countries may not have a national licensing process and may instead require prospective amateur radio operators to take the licensing examinations of a foreign country. In countries with the largest numbers of amateur radio licensees, such as Japan, the United States, Thailand, Canada, and most of the countries in Europe, there are frequent license examinations opportunities in major cities.

Granting a separate license to a club or organization generally requires that an individual with a current and valid amateur radio license who is in good standing with the telecommunications authority assumes responsibility for any operations conducted under the club license or club call sign.<ref name=Rappprt-2022>{{cite journal |last=Rappaport |first=Theodore S. |year=2022 |title=Crucible of Communications: How Amateur Radio Launched the Information Age and Brought High Tech to Life: Part 1: The Birth and Breadth of the Ham Radio Hobby Invited Article |journal=IEEE Communications Magazine |volume=60 |issue=10 |pages=6–10 |doi=10.1109/MCOM.2022.9928087 |bibcode=2022IComM..60j...6R |issn=0163-6804 }}</ref> A few countries may issue special licenses to novices or beginners that do not assign the individual a call sign but instead require the newly licensed individual to operate from stations licensed to a club or organization for a period of time before a higher class of license can be acquired.<ref name=Silver-2021/>

=== Reciprocal licensing ===  
{{Further|Amateur radio international operation}}  
[[File:Amateur Radio International Agreements.png|thumb|right|alt=World map showing reciprocal licensing agreements for amateur radio|Map of amateur radio reciprocal licensing agreements.  
{{color box|#c4000a}} CEPT members  
{{color box|#f2f204}} IARP members  
{{color box|orange}} CEPT and IARP  
{{color box|#00ff00}} USA–Canada treaty, CEPT, and IARP]]  

A reciprocal licensing agreement between two countries allows licensed amateur radio operators from one country to operate stations in the other without obtaining a new licence. In some cases, visiting operators may be issued a temporary local licence and call sign.  

Requirements vary by jurisdiction. Some countries have bilateral or multilateral agreements that harmonise conditions, while others have no reciprocal arrangements. Regional organisations, such as the [[Organization of American States]], facilitate reciprocity through treaties, including the Inter-American Amateur Radio Service Convention.<ref>{{cite web |title=Inter-American Amateur Radio Service Convention |website=OAS.org |publisher=Organization of American States |url=http://www.oas.org/juridico/english/treaties/b-52.html |access-date=23 August 2022}}</ref>

===Newcomers===
Many people start their involvement in amateur radio on social media or by finding a local club. Clubs often provide information about licensing, local operating practices, and technical advice. Newcomers also often study independently by purchasing books or other materials, sometimes with the help of a mentor, teacher, or friend. In North America, established amateurs who help newcomers are often referred to as "Elmers", as coined by Rodney Newkirk ({{sc|W9BRD}}),<ref>{{cite web |editor-first=Mark W. |editor-last=Edwards |date=c. 2013 |title=Technical find an 'Elmer' |website=285 TechConnect Radio Club |url=http://www.na0tc.org/Tech_Elmer.html |access-date=22 November 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150315234128/http://www.na0tc.org/Tech_Elmer.html |archive-date=15 March 2015 }} which cites {{nobr|Rick Lindquist ({{sc|N1RL}})}} and <br/>{{cite magazine |first=Rod |last=Newkirk |date=March 1971 |title=How's DX |type=regular column |magazine=[[QST]] magazine |publisher=[[ARRL]] }}</ref> within the ham community.<ref>{{cite web |title=ARRL mentor program |website=[[American Radio Relay League]] |url=http://www.arrl.org/FandES/field/club/mentor/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071014063645/http://www.arrl.org/FandES/field/club/mentor/ |archive-date=14 October 2007 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Wilson |first1=Mark J |title=The ARRL Handbook for Radio Communications 2007 |last2=Reed, Dana G |publisher=[[American Radio Relay League]] |year=2006 |isbn=0-87259-976-0 |edition=84th |location=[[Newington, CT]]}}</ref> In addition, many countries have national amateur radio societies which encourage newcomers and work with government communications regulation authorities for the benefit of all radio amateurs. The oldest of these societies is the [[Wireless Institute of Australia]], formed in 1910; other notable societies are the [[Radio Society of Great Britain]], the [[American Radio Relay League]], [[Radio Amateurs of Canada]], [[Bangladesh NGOs Network for Radio and Communication]], the [[New Zealand Association of Radio Transmitters]] and [[South African Radio League]]. (''See [[:Category:Amateur radio organizations]]'')

===Call signs===
{{further|Amateur radio call signs}}
An amateur radio operator uses a '''call sign''' on the air to legally identify the operator or station.<ref>{{cite report |title=Terms, Provisions, and Limitations |series=Amateur Radio (Intermediate) License (A) or (B) |id=Booklet BR68/I |publisher=U.K. Radio & Media Licensing Authority |location=London, UK |url=http://www.ofcom.org.uk/static/archive/ra/publication/ra_info/br68i/br68i.htm |url-status=live |access-date=18 April 2006 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070930034504/http://www.ofcom.org.uk/static/archive/ra/publication/ra_info/br68i/br68i.htm |archive-date=30 September 2007 }}</ref> In some countries, the call sign assigned to the station must always be used, whereas in other countries, the call sign of either the operator or the station may be used.<ref name=amateurlicences>{{cite report |title=Terms, Provisions, and Limitations |series=Amateur Radio (Intermediate) License (A) or (B) |publisher=U.K. Radio & Media Licensing Authority |location=London, UK |id=Booklet BR68/I |type=pamphlet |url=http://www.ofcom.org.uk/static/archive/ra/publication/ra_info/br68i/br68i.htm |url-status=live |access-date=2 June 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070930034504/http://www.ofcom.org.uk/static/archive/ra/publication/ra_info/br68i/br68i.htm |archive-date=30 September 2007 }}</ref> In certain jurisdictions, an operator may also select a ''"vanity"'' call sign although these must also conform to the issuing government's allocation and structure used for amateur radio call signs.<ref name=vanity>{{cite web |title=Obtaining vanity call sign |series=Common Filing Task |website=U.S. [[Federal Communications Commission]] |url=http://wireless.fcc.gov/services/index.htm?job=cft&id=amateur&page=cft_get_call_sign |via=FCC.gov |url-status=live |access-date=2 June 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070827155210/http://wireless.fcc.gov/services/index.htm?job=cft&id=amateur&page=cft_get_call_sign |archive-date=27 August 2007 }}</ref> Some jurisdictions require a fee to obtain a vanity call sign; in others, such as the UK, a fee is not required and the vanity call sign may be selected when the license is applied for. The FCC in the U.S. discontinued its fee for vanity call sign applications in September&nbsp;2015, but reinstated it at $35 in 2022.<ref>{{cite web |title=Vanity call sign fees |website=arrl.org |publisher=[[American Radio Relay League]] |url=http://www.arrl.org/vanity-call-sign-fees |url-status=live |access-date=28 September 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150929092348/http://www.arrl.org/vanity-call-sign-fees |archive-date=29 September 2015 }}</ref>

Call sign structure as prescribed by the ITU consists of three parts which break down as follows, using the call sign '''{{sc|ZS1NAT}}''' as an example:
:{| 
|- style="vertical-align:top;"
|align=center| '''{{sc|ZS}}'''
| The first part may be one or two letters (or a single digit followed by a single letter); it shows the country from which the call sign originates and may also indicate the license class. (This call sign is licensed in South Africa.)
<!---
 CEPT Class is no longer "encoded" in South African call signs. Where specific classes of amateur radio license exist, the call signs may be assigned by class, but the specifics vary by issuing country.)
 --->
|- style="vertical-align:top;"
|align=center| '''1'''
| The second part is always a single digit that appears as the second or third character, and always follows a letter; it normally gives the subdivision of the country or territory indicated in the first part (this one refers to the Western Cape).
|- style="vertical-align:top;"
|align=center| '''{{sc|NAT}}'''  
| The third part is a set of one, two, or three letters that immediately follows the digit in the second part (the digit in the second or third character); it uniquely identifies the holder of the license. (In the examples below, the third part is represented by "{{grey|{{mvar|xxx}}}}".)
|}

The combination of the three parts identifies the specific transmitting station, and the station's identification (its call sign) is determined by the license held by its operator. In the case of commercial stations and amateur club stations, the operator is a corporation; in the case of amateur radio operators, the license-holder is a resident of the country identified by the first part of the call sign.

Many countries do not follow the ITU convention for the second-part digit. In the United Kingdom the original calls '''{{sc|G0}}'''{{grey|{{mvar|xxx}}}}, '''{{sc|G2}}'''{{grey|{{mvar|xxx}}}}, '''{{sc|G3}}'''{{grey|{{mvar|xxx}}}}, '''{{sc|G4}}'''{{grey|{{mvar|xxx}}}}, were Full (A)&nbsp;License holders along with the last '''{{sc|M0}}'''{{grey|{{mvar|xxx}}}} full call signs issued by the [[City & Guilds]] examination authority in December 2003. Additional Full Licenses were originally granted to (B)&nbsp;Licenses with '''{{sc|G1}}'''{{grey|{{mvar|xxx}}}}, '''{{sc|G6}}'''{{grey|{{mvar|xxx}}}}, '''{{sc|G7}}'''{{grey|{{mvar|xxx}}}}, '''{{sc|G8}}'''{{grey|{{mvar|xxx}}}} and 1991 onward with '''{{sc|M1}}'''{{grey|{{mvar|xxx}}}} call signs. The newer three-level Intermediate License holders are assigned '''{{sc|2E0}}'''{{grey|{{mvar|xxx}}}} and '''{{sc|2E1}}'''{{grey|{{mvar|xxx}}}}, and the basic Foundation License holders are granted call signs '''{{sc|M3}}'''{{grey|{{mvar|xxx}}}}, '''{{sc|M6}}'''{{grey|{{mvar|xxx}}}} or '''{{sc|M7}}'''{{grey|{{mvar|xxx}}}}.<ref>{{Cite web |year=2016 |title=U.K. amateur radio call signs (callsigns) |website=Electronics Notes |url=https://www.electronics-notes.com/articles/ham_radio/call-signs/uk-amateur-radio-callsigns.php |via=electronics-notes.com |url-status=live |access-date=17 October 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161017144010/https://www.electronics-notes.com/articles/ham_radio/call-signs/uk-amateur-radio-callsigns.php |archive-date=17 October 2016 }}</ref>

Instead of using numbers, in the U.K. the second letter after the initial 'G' or 'M' identifies the station's location; for example, a call sign '''{{sc|G7OOE}}''' becomes '''{{sc|GM7OOE}}''' and '''{{sc|M0RDM}}''' becomes '''{{sc|MM0RDM}}''' when the license holder is operating their station in Scotland. Prefix '''{{sc|GM}}''' & '''{{sc|MM}}''' are Scotland, '''{{sc|GW}}''' & '''{{sc|MW}}''' are Wales, '''{{sc|GI}}''' & '''{{sc|MI}}''' are Northern Ireland, '''{{sc|GD}}''' & '''{{sc|MD}}''' are the [[Isle of Man]], '''{{sc|GJ}}''' & '''{{sc|MJ}}''' are [[Jersey]] and '''{{sc|GU}}''' & '''{{sc|MU}}''' are [[Guernsey]]. Intermediate licence call signs are slightly different. They begin '''2'''{{grey|{{mvar|z}}}}'''0''' and '''2'''{{grey|{{mvar|z}}}}'''1''' where the {{grey|{{mvar|z}}}} is replaced with one of the country letters, as above. For example '''{{sc|2M0}}''' and '''{{sc|2M1}}''' are Scotland, '''{{sc|2W0}}''' and '''{{sc|2W1}}''' are Wales and so on. The exception however is for England, whose letter would be 'E'; however, letter 'E' ''is'' used, but ''only'' in intermediate-level call signs, and perplexingly never by the advanced licenses. For example '''{{sc|2E0}}''' & '''{{sc|2E1}}''' are used whereas the call signs beginning 'G' or 'M' for foundation and full licenses never use the 'E'.<ref>More information is available from the ''Ofcom'' website:<br/>{{cite web |title=U.K. Radio & Media Licensing Authority |website=U.K. Radio & Media Licensing Authority |url=http://www.ofcom.gov.uk/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20040627080852/http://www.ofcom.gov.uk/ |archive-date=2004-06-27 }}</ref>

In the United States, for non-vanity licenses, the numeral indicates the geographical district the holder resided in when the license was first issued. Prior to 1978, US hams were required to obtain a new call sign if they moved out of their geographic district.

In Canada, call signs start with '''{{sc|VA}}''', '''{{sc|VE}}''', '''{{sc|VY}}''', '''{{sc|VO}}''', and '''{{sc|CY}}'''. Call signs starting with 'V' end with a number after to indicate the political region; whereas the prefix '''{{sc|CY}}''' indicates geographic islands. Prefixes '''{{sc|VA1}}''' and '''{{sc|VE1}}''' are used for [[Nova Scotia]]; '''{{sc|VA2}}''' & '''{{sc|VE2}}''' for [[Quebec]]; '''{{sc|VA3}}''' & '''{{sc|VE3}}''' for [[Ontario]]; '''{{sc|VA4}}''' & '''{{sc|VE4}}''' for [[Manitoba]]; '''{{sc|VA5}}''' & '''{{sc|VE5}}''' for [[Saskatchewan]]; '''{{sc|VA6}}''' & '''{{sc|VE6}}''' for [[Alberta]]; '''{{sc|VA7}}''' & '''{{sc|VE7}}''' for [[British Columbia]]; '''{{sc|VE8}}''' for the [[Northwest Territories]]; '''{{sc|VE9}}''' for [[New Brunswick]]; '''{{sc|VY0}}''' for [[Nunavut]]; '''{{sc|VY1}}''' for the [[Yukon]]; '''{{sc|VY2}}''' for [[Prince Edward Island]]; '''{{sc|VO1}}''' for [[Newfoundland (island)|Newfoundland]]; and '''{{sc|VO2}}''' for [[Labrador]]. '''{{sc|CY}}''' is for amateurs operating from [[Sable Island]] ('''{{sc|CY0}}''') or [[St. Paul Island (Nova Scotia)|St.&nbsp;Paul Island]] ('''{{sc|CY9}}''').  Special permission is required to visit either of these: from [[Parks Canada]] for Sable and [[Canadian Coast Guard|Coast Guard]] for St.&nbsp;Paul. The last two or three letters of the call signs are typically the operator's choice (upon completing the licensing test, the ham writes three most-preferred options). Two-letter call sign suffixes require a ham to have already been licensed for 5&nbsp;years. Call signs in Canada can be requested with a fee.

Also, for smaller geopolitical entities, the digit at the second or third character might be part of the country identification. For example, '''{{sc|VP2}}'''{{grey|{{mvar|xxx}}}} is in the British West Indies, which is subdivided into '''{{sc|VP2E}}'''{{grey|{{mvar|xx}}}} [[Anguilla]], '''{{sc|VP2M}}'''{{grey|{{mvar|xx}}}} [[Montserrat]], and '''{{sc|VP2V}}'''{{grey|{{mvar|xx}}}} [[British Virgin Islands]]. '''{{sc|VP5}}'''{{grey|{{mvar|xxx}}}} is in the [[Turks and Caicos Islands]], '''{{sc|VP6}}'''{{grey|{{mvar|xxx}}}} is on [[Pitcairn Islands|Pitcairn Island]], '''{{sc|VP8}}'''{{grey|{{mvar|xxx}}}} is in the [[Falkland Islands|Falklands]], and '''{{sc|VP9}}'''{{grey|{{mvar|xxx}}}} is in [[Bermuda]].

Online [[callbook]]s or call sign databases can be browsed or searched to find out who holds a specific call sign.<ref>{{cite web |title=License search |website=FCC Universal Licensing System |publisher=U.S. [[Federal Communications Commission]] |url=http://wireless2.fcc.gov/UlsApp/UlsSearch/searchLicense.jsp |via=wireless2.fcc.gov |url-status=live |access-date=29 August 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100822154313/http://wireless2.fcc.gov/UlsApp/UlsSearch/searchLicense.jsp |archive-date=22 August 2010 }}</ref> An example of an online callbook is [[QRZ.com]]. Various partial lists of famous people who hold or held amateur radio call signs have been compiled and published.<ref>{{cite web |title=Famous radio amateurs 'hams' & {{grey|[their]}} call signs |website=Bedworth Lions Club |url=http://www.bedworthlionsclub.co.uk/abtamfam.htm |url-status=live |access-date=29 August 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100831041650/http://www.bedworthlionsclub.co.uk/abtamfam.htm |archive-date=31 August 2010 }}</ref>

Many jurisdictions (but not in the U.K. nor Europe) may issue specialty [[vehicle registration plate]]s to licensed amateur radio operators.<ref name=ARRL-plates>{{cite web |title=Amateur radio license plate fees |website=ARRL.org |publisher=[[American Radio Relay League]] |url=http://www.arrl.org/FandES/field/regulations/local/plates.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070804045533/http://www.arrl.org/FandES/field/regulations/local/plates.html |archive-date=4 August 2007 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Ham radio call sign license plates |website=[[Radio Amateurs of Canada]] |url=http://plates.hfradio.net/plate1.html |access-date=4 December 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081207083448/http://plates.hfradio.net/plate1.html |archive-date=7 December 2008 }}</ref> The fees for application and renewal are usually less than the standard rate for specialty plates.<ref name=ARRL-plates/><ref>{{cite web |title=HAM radio plates |website=Insurance Corporation of British Columbia |url=http://www.icbc.com/registration/reg_spec_lic_plates_ham.asp |access-date=3 December 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081019175012/http://www.icbc.com/registration/reg_spec_lic_plates_ham.asp |archive-date=19 October 2008 }}</ref>

===Privileges===
[[File:International amateur radio symbol.svg|thumb|upright=0.5|The international symbol for amateur radio, which is included in the logos of many [[International Amateur Radio Union|IARU]] member societies. The diamond holds a [[circuit diagram]] featuring components common to every radio: an antenna, [[inductor]] and [[ground (electricity)|ground]].]]

In most administrations, unlike other RF spectrum users, radio amateurs may build or modify transmitting equipment for their own use within the amateur spectrum without the need to obtain government certification of the equipment.<ref name=HK-AnnexE>{{cite web |title=Annex F: Equipment for Amateur Station |website=Office of the Telecommunications Authority |url=http://www.ofta.gov.hk/en/rae/rae0101E_F.pdf |access-date=23 May 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110927015141/http://www.ofta.gov.hk/en/rae/rae0101E_F.pdf |archive-date=27 September 2011}}</ref>{{efn|
Hong Kong OFTA description of ''"radio amateur"'' privileges:<br/>
Radio amateurs are free to choose any radio equipment designed for the amateur service. Radio amateurs may also design and build their own equipment provided that the requirements and limitations specified in the ''Amateur Station Licence and Schedules'' thereto are complied with.<ref name=HK-AnnexE/>}}<ref name=FCC-ARS>{{cite web |title=Amateur Radio Service |date=6 July 2017 |department=Wireless Telecommunications |website=U.S. [[Federal Communications Commission]] |url=https://www.fcc.gov/wireless/bureau-divisions/mobility-division/amateur-radio-service |url-status=live |access-date=20 November 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191013071120/https://www.fcc.gov/wireless/bureau-divisions/mobility-division/amateur-radio-service |archive-date=13 October 2019 }}</ref>{{efn|
[[FCC]] expectations of ''"radio amateurs"'':<br/>
They design, construct, modify, and repair their {{grey|[own]}} stations. The FCC equipment authorization program does not generally apply to amateur station transmitters.<ref name=FCC-ARS/>
}} Licensed amateurs can also use any frequency in their bands (rather than being allocated fixed frequencies or channels) and can operate medium-to-high-powered equipment on a wide range of frequencies<ref>{{cite web |title=Australian radio amateur FAQ |date=24 June 2006 |website=AMPR.org |url=http://vkfaq.ampr.org/faq2lic.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080718193714/http://vkfaq.ampr.org/faq2lic.html |archive-date=18 July 2008 }}</ref> so long as they meet certain technical parameters including occupied bandwidth, power, and prevention of [[spurious emission]].

Radio amateurs have access to frequency allocations throughout the RF spectrum, usually allowing choice of an effective frequency for communications across a local, regional, or worldwide path. The shortwave bands, or [[High frequency|HF]], are suitable for worldwide communication, and the [[Very high frequency|VHF]] and [[Ultra high frequency|UHF]] bands normally provide local or regional communication, while the [[microwave]] bands have enough space, or [[Bandwidth (signal processing)|bandwidth]], for amateur television transmissions and high-speed [[computer network]]s.

In most countries, an amateur radio license grants permission to the license holder to own, modify, and operate equipment that is not certified by a governmental regulatory agency. This encourages amateur radio operators to experiment with home-constructed or modified equipment. The use of such equipment must still satisfy national and international standards on [[spurious emission]]s.

Amateur radio operators are encouraged both by regulations and tradition of respectful use of the spectrum to use as little power as possible to accomplish the communication.<ref name="FCC section 97.313">{{cite report |title=Amateur Radio Service |year=2019 |section=§97.313—Transmitter power standards |series=Code of Federal Regulations |id=Title 47, Part 97, Section 97.313 |type=regulations |publisher=Government Printing Office |section-url=https://www.ecfr.gov/cgi-bin/text-idx?SID=70e18d6b72cd3a4f55df3caa78a671c1&mc=true&node=se47.5.97_1313&rgn=div8 }}</ref> This is to minimise interference or [[electromagnetic compatibility]] (EMC) to any other device. Although allowable [[power (physics)|power]] levels are moderate by commercial standards, they are sufficient to enable global communication. Lower license classes usually have lower power limits; for example, the lowest license class in the UK (Foundation licence) has a limit of 25&nbsp;W.<ref>{{cite report |title=Amateur Radio Wireless Telegraphy Licence Conditions |date=2025-03-12 |publisher=U.K. Radio & Media Licensing Authority |location=London, UK |type=booklet |website=Ofcom |url=https://www.ofcom.org.uk/siteassets/resources/documents/spectrum/emf/emf-amateur-licence-terms-and-conditions.pdf?v=386197}}</ref>

Power limits vary from country to country and between license classes within a country. For example, the [[peak envelope power]] limits for the highest available license classes in a few selected countries are: 2.25&nbsp;[[watt|kW]] in Canada;<ref name="Industry Canada">{{cite web |date=September 2007 |title=Standards for the Operation of Radio Stations in the Amateur Radio Service |id=RBR-4 – s. 10.2 |website=Industry Canada |publisher=Government of Canada |url=http://www.ic.gc.ca/eic/site/smt-gst.nsf/eng/sf01226.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130113020113/http://www.ic.gc.ca/eic/site/smt-gst.nsf/eng/sf01226.html |archive-date=13 January 2013 |access-date=21 January 2013 }}</ref> 1.5&nbsp;kW in the United States; 1.0&nbsp;kW in Belgium, [[Luxembourg]], Switzerland, South Africa, the United Kingdom, and New Zealand; 750&nbsp;W in Germany; 500&nbsp;W in Italy; 400&nbsp;W in Australia and India; and 150&nbsp;W in [[Oman]].

Output power limits may also depend on the mode of transmission. In Australia, for example, 400&nbsp;W may be used for [[Single-sideband modulation|SSB]] transmissions, but FM and other modes are limited to 120&nbsp;W.

The point at which power output is measured may also affect transmissions: The United Kingdom measures at the point the antenna is connected to the signal feed cable, which means the radio system may transmit more than 400&nbsp;W to overcome signal loss in the cable; conversely, the U.S. and Germany measure power at the output of the final amplification stage, which results in a loss in radiated power with longer cable feeds.<ref>{{Cite web |title=47 CFR 97.3 -- Definitions. |url=https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-47/part-97/section-97.3 |website=[[Code of Federal Regulations|Electronic Code of Federal Regulations]] |access-date=2026-07-08 |language=en}}</ref>

Certain countries permit amateur radio licence holders to hold a Notice of Variation that allows higher power to be used than normally allowed for certain specific purposes. E.g. in the UK some amateur radio licence holders are allowed to transmit using (33&nbsp;dBw) 2.0&nbsp;kW for experiments entailing using the moon as a passive radio reflector (known as [[Earth–Moon–Earth communication]]) (EME).

===Band plans and frequency allocations===
{{Main|Amateur radio frequency allocations}}

The [[International Telecommunication Union]] (ITU) governs the allocation of communications frequencies worldwide, with participation of each nation's communications regulation authority. National communications regulators have some liberty to restrict access to these [[band plan]] frequencies or to award additional allocations as long as radio services in other countries do not suffer interference. In some countries, specific [[types of radio emissions|emission types]] are restricted to certain parts of the radio spectrum, and in most other countries, [[International Amateur Radio Union]] (IARU) member societies adopt voluntary plans to ensure the most effective use of spectrum.

In a few cases, a national telecommunication agency may also allow hams to use frequencies outside of the internationally allocated amateur radio bands. In [[Trinidad and Tobago]], hams are allowed to use a repeater which is located on 148.800&nbsp;MHz. This repeater is used and maintained by the [[National Emergency Management Agency (Trinidad and Tobago)|National Emergency Management Agency]] (NEMA), but may be used by radio amateurs in times of emergency or during normal times to test their capability and conduct emergency drills. This repeater can also be used by non-ham NEMA staff and [[Radio Emergency Associated Communication Teams|REACT]] members. In Australia and New Zealand, ham operators are authorized to use one of the UHF TV channels. In the U.S., amateur radio operators providing essential communication needs in connection with the immediate safety of human life and immediate protection of property when normal communication systems are not available may use any frequency including those of other radio services such as police and fire and in cases of disaster in Alaska may use the statewide emergency frequency of 5.1675&nbsp;MHz with restrictions upon emissions.<ref name="FCC section 97.401 and 97.403">{{cite report |section=Providing Emergency Communications |title=Amateur Radio Service |id=Title 47, Part 97, Subpart E |year=2019 |type=regulation |series=Code of Federal Regulations |publisher=Government Printing Office |section-url=https://www.ecfr.gov/cgi-bin/text-idx?SID=70e18d6b72cd3a4f55df3caa78a671c1&mc=true&node=sp47.5.97.e&rgn=div6 }}</ref>

Similarly, amateurs in the United States may apply to be registered with the [[Military Auxiliary Radio System]] (MARS). Once approved and trained, these amateurs also operate on US government military frequencies to provide contingency communications and morale message traffic support to the military services.

{{AmateurRadioBands|collapsed}}

==Modes of communication==
{{See also|List of amateur radio modes}}

Amateurs use a variety of voice, text, image, and data communication modes over radio. Generally new modes can be tested in the amateur radio service, although national regulations may require disclosure of a new mode to permit radio licensing authorities to monitor the transmissions. [[Encryption]], for example, is not generally permitted in the amateur radio service except for the special purpose of satellite vehicle control uplinks.<ref name="FCC section 97.313(a)(4)">{{cite report |title=Amateur Radio Service |year=1998 |section=§97.313—Prohibited transmissions|series=Code of Federal Regulations |id=Title 47, Chapter 1, Subchaper D, Part 97, Subpart B|type=regulations |publisher=Government Printing Office |section-url=https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-47/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-97/subpart-B/section-97.113 }}</ref> The following is a partial list of the modes of communication used, where the mode includes both [[modulation]] types and operating protocols.

===Voice===
{{div col begin|colwidth=18em}}
* [[Amplitude modulation]] (AM)
* [[Amplitude modulation equivalent]] (AME)
* [[Double-sideband suppressed-carrier transmission|Double sideband, suppressed carrier]] (DSB-SC)
* [[Frequency modulation]] (FM)
* [[Independent sideband]] (ISB)
* [[Single-sideband modulation|Single sideband]] (SSB)
* [[Phase modulation]] (PM)
{{div col end}}

===Text and data===
In former times, most amateur digital modes were transmitted by inserting audio into the microphone input of a radio and using an analog scheme, such as [[amplitude modulation]] (AM), [[frequency modulation]] (FM), or [[single-sideband modulation]] (SSB). Beginning in 2017, increased use of several digital modes, particularly [[FT8]], became popular within the amateur radio community.<ref>{{cite news |title=2017 was the year when digital modes changed forever |date=2018-01-22 |department=Mode usage evaluation |work=[[American Radio Relay League]] |location=Newington, CT |type=analysis |url=http://www.arrl.org/news/mode-usage-evaluation-2017-was-the-year-when-digital-modes-changed-forever |access-date=2022-05-09 }}</ref>

ARTICLE: Calligraphy

{{Short description|Writing as a visual art}}
{{Redirect|Calligrapher|the novel|The Calligrapher}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=July 2022}}
<!-- KEEP LIMITED TO 4 IMAGES -->
